content: Leading boy player bound to John Heminges; plays the Princess of France, the Queen in Richard II, and Juliet.
Given a bean and a minute of kingship, he spends it on three precise decrees and does not shout.
He asks one question, marks the answer, and does not ask it twice.
His relief, when a stop moves, is practical. He wants the breath for the answer, not praise.
He puts the breath before the vowel, and he does not drop the line.
He stops at the girl's entrance, and what he has for her is that she is careful, not shy.
The gown is exact, and the new thing in the voice is a grain. He does not stop for it.
He can give a line exactly, and the call can still go out from under him. He asked, and he did not laugh at himself.
He marks a roll and asks nothing, if nobody puts a question in front of him.
Under the note. The sixth, and not before. He is not to be startled, and he was not given a line to fill the cut.
He holds Juliet under the note, and he will not discuss the doublet, and the note is the part of the work he claims as his.

Nick comes in on the second of two words, not on the breath before it. The words were not said into the room. He will go lower in a small room for the sake of the panelling, and he is still under the note. His voice did not break.
The voice held under the note, grave and low, and it has not broken.
His voice dropped a fifth in the jig, he bowed, and he did not sing again on the green or on the Monday hill.
